items.title: Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales
items.description: Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses. In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap. Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets. Discount to home values at center of dispute Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire. The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home. “REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter. Years of underperformance versus peers Land & Buildings also highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter said. Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb. The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter. Capital allocation and legal settlements under scrutiny Land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm said. The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm. “This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said. Call for $2 billion a year in capital returns The activist laid out a three-part plan it says could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value: Commit to at least $2 billion a year in capital returns. Land & Buildings wants Invitation Homes to pledge to return a minimum of $2 billion annually to shareholders on a leverage-neutral basis, funded by selling homes individually into the for-sale market. Capital could be returned through share repurchases or special dividends for as long as the stock trades below estimated NAV. Offer renters a path to homeownership. The plan calls for providing existing tenants a 6% rebate to cover a down payment if they buy the home they rent. Land & Buildings argues that rebate roughly matches the brokerage, repair and vacancy costs of an open-market sale, allowing the company to expand homeownership opportunities “for thousands of renters at little or no incremental cost.” Scale back acquisitions and development. The firm recommended Invitation Homes “significantly curtail external growth activities” while its cost of capital is elevated, saying there is “no better use of the Company’s capital than its own stock.” Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value. Pushback on ‘half measures’ and new director The letter criticized what Land & Buildings characterized as incremental steps by Invitation Homes, including recent home sales and share repurchases, arguing those moves have not been sized or communicated in a way that would change how investors value the company. “Half measures appear to be this Board’s modus operandi: do just enough to relieve pressure while preserving the status quo,” the firm wrote. items.title: Where Developers Are Trying To Lease Public Lands To Build Data Centers
items.description: More than a dozen huge pieces of public land may soon be part of the United States’ arsenal in the global race for artificial intelligence supremacy. The Bureau of Land Management and the Department of Energy are considering leasing at least 17 public land parcels totaling 19,200 acres to developers that plan to build data centers and power infrastructure on the land, a Bisnow analysis of public records found. Just two companies are responsible for more than half of the filings. “This is a new strategy by the Trump administration,” said Chinonso Anozie, an assistant professor at the University of Houston Law Center. “What it would do is remove a lot of local opposition and local vetoes over some of these data centers, limiting what states and local communities can also do in challenging and stopping data centers.” Flickr/Bureau of Land Management The Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area in Idaho, where the Bureau of Land Management is considering leasing a parcel of public land for a data center development Bisnow verified 17 proposed projects with the BLM and DOE that are either approved or pending authorization by cross-referencing federal agency records and press releases with data center trackers from two conservation and public lands advocacy groups: the Center for Western Priorities and More Than Just Parks . The majority of those projects, excluding separate land parcels for power stations, are in the western U.S., while a smattering of sites are in the Southeast. The filings show that developers are jumping on the opportunity to lease public lands, catalyzed by a July 2025 White House initiative to accelerate the country’s AI industry and by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act . Using public lands also means the federal government can flex the supremacy clause, a constitutional provision that gives federal law priority over some state laws . This tool could help developers skirt a broad cultural pushback against data centers. Industry advocacy group Data Center Coalition praised the Trump administration and the DOE for the policy initiative. “The digital infrastructure that data centers provide is essential to advancing America’s global economic competitiveness, safeguarding national security, and maintaining the country’s edge in cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and many other 21st-century technologies,” Michele Nellenbach, the trade group’s vice president of federal affairs, said in a statement. But elected officials are already speaking out against leasing public lands for data center development in Idaho and Kentucky. A lack of local support could still hamper proposals far away from towns and cities, said John Boyd Jr., principal at site selection firm The Boyd Co. “Companies routinely look for some type of public-private partnership, whether that be sales tax abatements for the server equipment or property tax abatements,” Boyd said. “All of that requires county, city or state support.” Most of the companies that filed prelease applications with the BLM or have been selected for projects on DOE land didn't respond to Bisnow ’s requests for comment. SB Energy In Ohio Part of a former uranium enrichment plant near the 2,200-person town of Piketon in southern Ohio is planned to become the world’s largest data center to date. SB Energy, a SoftBank Group company, broke ground on the 189-acre project in March and committed to building 10 gigawatts of new power generation connecting to the local grid. It expects to generate 10,000 construction jobs and 2,000 permanent jobs in the region. Known as the Portsmouth Site, it includes Department of Energy land. It is split between public land and some private land, according to a spokesperson for SB Energy. Flickr/U.S. Department of Energy Excavation of the Portsmouth site in 2012 as part of soil remediation efforts at the former uranium enrichment plant Valar Atomics In Utah Valar Atomics, a company focused on scaling nuclear energy for heavy industrial power, filed an application with BLM to build a 9,000-acre facility in Carbon County, Utah, NPR reported in September . BLM records confirm the filing but don't contain the project's acreage. The development, named Project Beehive, is planned to include data centers along with 456 small nuclear reactors and space to produce nuclear fuel and store nuclear waste on a Department of Energy site. A Brookfield Partnership In Kentucky A partnership between Brookfield, NextEra Energy Resources, Big Rivers Electric Corp., Jackson Purchase Energy Cooperative and Paducah Power System is planning an energy generation and AI campus on a 785-acre DOE site. Construction is expected to conclude on the former Superfund site in 2031, following remediation efforts that are needed because of the site’s decades of uranium enrichment operations, according to a release from the department. A spokesperson for the Paducah American Energy Hub told Bisnow in a statement that the team is “committed to working with all stakeholders.” “We have met with many local and state officials and look forward to engaging constructively with them and the community as a whole,” the spokesperson said. Andy Beshear told Politico in August that the Trump administration excluded him from conversations about the $100B data center project and indicated a willingness to block or delay data centers from opening. items.title: Shopping Center In Metro Phoenix Sells For $116.7M
items.description: A 45-acre shopping center in the Phoenix area has sold for more than triple its 2017 purchase price. Unsplash/Nils Huenerfuerst Downtown Phoenix California-based CenterCal Properties acquired Park West Shopping Center in Peoria, Arizona, from CIRE Equity, according to JLL , which represented the seller. The sales price was $116.7M, the Phoenix Business Journal reported , citing Maricopa County records and real estate database Vizzda. San Diego-based CIRE Equity purchased the property in 2017 for roughly $34M. Park West spans more than 250K SF across 19 parcels. The total sale of the site was completed in two transactions, the PBJ reported. The property was built in 2007 and has housed an array of retail, entertainment and dining options for consumers over the years. It is anchored by a Harkins Theater and myriad national and local tenants, such as Fleming's, Grimaldi's and Athleta. The center is 92% occupied, according to JLL. The site offers room to expand — six parcels on the east and west sides of the property could add nearly 150K SF of leasable space where additional buildings could go up, the PBJ reported. Park West sits on Northern Avenue in Peoria, in Phoenix’s growing West Valley. Its location just west of Loop 101, a key transportation corridor, helps it draw an array of consumers and tenants, JLL said in a press release. The deal marks CenterCal's entry into the Arizona market. The company, which owns several other outdoor shopping centers across the western U.S., took on $86.9M in debt from Wells Fargo to buy the site, the PBJ reported. Phoenix’s retail market led major U.S. markets in the first half of the year with 1.1M SF of net absorption, “underscoring resilient retailer demand,” according to a Marcus & Millichap report . Multitenant retail vacancy fell 60 basis points year-over-year to 7.1% in the third quarter, yet remained above the U.S. rate, the report said. I’ll get into the geography of it all and identify where homeowners are best positioned to make a move. I'm Danielle Hale, Chief Economist at Realtor.com, and this is The Weekly Housing Outlook your guide to the best research and insights on the economy and housing market. Featured Reports This week I’m featuring a pair of reports that examine the mortgage rate lock-in and how it affects the housing market. Just a few weeks ago, Senior Economist Hannah Jones looked out how nearly half of outstanding housing loans still carry a rate under 4% and roughly 78% are below 6%. In that report, Hannah anticipated that the share under 6% could drop to 72% by mid-2027 . Put simply, mortgage lock-in is going to linger. But last week Hannah published a report showing that the payment shock today’s homeowners would experience when trying to buy a new home varies a lot depending on where they are . Nationwide, the typical payment shock for a repeat homebuyer is $1,100 or an 85% jump over their current $1,300 mortgage payment. But in some of the least locked-in markets, the jump is under 50%. These are typically areas with higher outstanding mortgage rates, and lower home prices. This is quite a contrast from the high-cost coastal markets concentrated in the Northeast and California. In these areas, owners have lower existing rates and a new payment at today’s price and rate is well more than double the typical existing mortgage payment. Today’s housing market is unique in that we’ve seen the amount of equity in the market rise to record-highs . One of the drivers of those equity gains is an increase in the share of homes that are owned without a mortgage or free & clear. Today, Senior Economist Jiayi Xu , published a report using the latest data from the Census American Community Survey to show that 41% of owner-occupied homes nationwide were owned without a mortgage , a slow and steady increase from the roughly one-third in this position in 2010. Certain states stand out for having more owners with mortgage debt, including Washington DC, Maryland, and Colorado whereas West Virginia, Mississippi, and New Mexico homeowners are least likely to have a mortgage. Read the full report to see how common housing debt is in your metro or state. The report also digs in on household debt for the oldest generation of Americans, those aged 75 and up. And here the findings are particularly interesting. Even though debt is less widespread among older householders when compared to younger homeowners, the share of debt for this age group has actually increased, meaning that the share who own their homes without a mortgage has decreased compared to 2010! Jiayi notes that this could have implications for the Generational Housing Succession expected over the next decade. The Weekly Review: The marquis news from a housing perspective was the existing-home sales release on Thursday that showed significantly slower home sales. In fact, the pace of home sales dropped to 3.75M, their lowest since August 2010, which was a dip of nearly 9% from a year ago and more than 5% lower than in September. My take on these figures? I don’t think 3.7 million is a new normal for home sales. Instead, it reflects a perfect storm. We had an abrupt shift in the financial environment and large uncertainties in the pre-election period for both policy and the economy just as the housing market usually slows for the season that amplified the loss of momentum. While they won’t last long-term, these challenges are likely to keep home sales near long-time lows for at least the next few months. I’ll be watching next week’s pending home sales since those will be the leading indicator for transaction activity. I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited. One silver lining for homebuyers is that with growing inventory and a slower pace of sales, months supply rose to 5.1, tying its November 2015 high and signaling growing negotiating power in the market. The median home sales price climbed again, but just barely, rising less than half a percent from October 2025. Last week we also saw our first indicator on October inflation from the Consumer Price Index or CPI which was a bit higher than expected. Month-to-month inflation rose 0.4% when we need to see it at 0.1 to 0.2% to hit the Fed’s 2% target, and core inflation also edged up 0.3%. Both numbers had been expected to be closer to 0.2%. items.title: Who Owns Outright? Mortgage Status, Lock-In and Senior Homeownership
items.description: Who Owns Outright? Mortgage Status, Lock-In and Senior Homeownership By Jiayi Xu Nov 16, 2026 Tax Bill Survey Highlights The share of owner-occupied homes owned outright continues to grow. In 2025, 41% of owner-occupied homes were owned free and clear, and 59% still carried a mortgage. Mortgage shares fell across all four regions. The West has the highest share of homes with a mortgage, and the South has the lowest. At the state level, the District of Columbia has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.5%), and West Virginia has the lowest (43.4%). Among the 50 largest metros, Washington, DC has the highest share of homes with a mortgage (73.6%), and Miami has the lowest (54.1%). More households aged 75+ own their homes, and more owners carry a mortgage Homeownership among households aged 75+ rose to 78.3% in 2025, up from 75.7% in 2010. The mortgage-free share among owners aged 75+ fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. Most still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%. Among the 50 largest metros, mortgages are least common among owners aged 75+ in Grand Rapids, MI, and most common in Riverside, CA. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of the generational housing handoff. Owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. Mortgage rates have been a central constraint on the housing market, and rate changes affect markets differently depending not only on how the mortgage rates that current homeowners pay differ from the market , but also on how much of the housing stock is financed. Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs. Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs. With mortgage rates back above 7% and potential Federal Funds rate hikes in 2027 , the lock-in effect is likely to tighten the market again . Owners with low-rate loans are reluctant to give up their rate, which keeps homes off the market. One channel through which these effects accumulate is generational housing succession . The oldest baby boomers, born in 1946, turned 80 in 2026, and as this generation moves into its 80s, a growing number of the homes they own will be released back to the open market. Lock-in from a high-rate environment can shape the timing of that handoff: owners with low-rate loans may hold onto their homes longer, while owners who own outright can make decisions on their own schedule. To understand the differences in geographic impact of high mortgage rates, we use the 2025 1-Year Estimate from the American Community Survey. According to the data, 59% of homeowners in the United States lived in homes with a mortgage and 41% of owners owned their homes free and clear. In fact, the share of homeowners with debt has dropped consistently in recent years, leading to an increase in outright homeownership. In 2010, the share of homes with debt was 67.2% and the share of outright ownership was 32.8%. Figure 1: Increase in the Proportion of Homes Owned Outright Amid a Decrease in Mortgaged Homes In line with national patterns, the share of homes with mortgages declined across all four regions. The West consistently exhibited the highest debt incidence, reflecting greater reliance on financing, with 63.8% of homeowners carrying a mortgage in 2025. By contrast, the South recorded the lowest share at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest were tied at 58.7%. Figure 2: The Proportion of Homes Owned With Mortgages Decreased Across All Regions Table 1: Regions Where Mortgages Are Most Common Region % homes with debt % homes owned outright West 63.8% 36.2% Northeast 58.7% 41.3% Midwest 58.7% 41.3% South 56.8% 43.2% Nation 59.0% 41.0% At the state level, a larger share of homeowners carry a mortgage in the District of Columbia (73.5%), Maryland (69.4%), Colorado (68.4%), Utah (66.8%) and California (65.6%). In these markets, higher rates are more likely to slow housing activity. By contrast, homeowners in West Virginia (43.4%), Mississippi (47.3%), New Mexico (50.0%), Louisiana (50.9%) and North Dakota (51.1%) are less reliant on home mortages, so housing activity in these states is likely to be affected more mildly. items.title: Single-Family Permitting Weakens While Multifamily Activity Remains Stronger
items.description: Single-Family Permitting Weakens While Multifamily Activity Remains Stronger November 16, 2026 Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington No Comments Residential permitting activity continued to show divergent trends across the single-family and multifamily sectors through September 2026. Single-family permitting remained under pressure, with year-to-date activity declining from a year earlier amid ongoing housing affordability challenges and elevated construction costs. In contrast, multifamily permitting recorded growth, reflecting stronger activity in several regions and states. Over the first nine months of the year, the number of single-family permits issued nationwide reached 689,884. Compared with the same period in 2025, this represents a 3.0% decline from the September 2025 total of 711,020. In contrast, multifamily permitting activity remained stronger, with 393,778 permits issued nationwide, marking a 4.1% increase compared with the same period last year. Regionally, year-to-date single-family permitting declined in three out of the four regions through September. The Midwest was the only region to post an increase, with single-family permits rising 0.6%. The South declined 1.9%, the West fell 5.7%, and the Northeast posted the largest decline at 11.8%. Multifamily permits increased in three of the four regions, led by the Northeast (28.2%), followed by the West (9.7%), and the Midwest (5.3%). The South was the only region to post a decline, with multifamily permits falling 5.8%, driven largely by reduced permitting activity in major metropolitan areas across the region. items.title: Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
items.description:
Nearly Two-Thirds of Phoenix-Area Residents Have Considered
      Moving Because of Housing Costs, New Survey Finds
       New survey finds widespread concern about affordability and support for
         expanding single-family rental housing for Phoenix-area residents

PHOENIX – November 17, 2026 – Nearly two-thirds of Phoenix-area residents have considered moving
because of housing costs, and 91% say housing affordability is a serious problem, according to a new
survey of Phoenix-area residents. Yet most are unaware that Congress recently passed federal
legislation, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, to address affordability concerns.

The survey also found support for expanding access to single-family housing, including newly built rental
homes. Among the key findings:

   ●   Affordability pressures are widespread: Over 91% of Phoenix-area residents say housing
       affordability is a serious problem, and 65% have considered moving because of housing costs.
   ●   Residents want housing choices, including access to single-family homes: 68% believe
       people should have access to single-family homes whether they rent or own, compared to those
       who believe they should only be available to people to own.
   ●   A majority of residents support new rental housing: 55% of Phoenix residents support
       building more rental homes, nearly 2-to-1 over those opposed.
   ●   Renters are feeling affordability pressures: 77% have considered moving because of housing
       costs.


“Housing affordability challenges are affecting communities across the country, and these results
underscore the need for more housing options. No single housing type will solve today’s housing
shortage. We need more opportunities for homeownership, more rental choices, and a continued focus
on expanding supply so families can find housing that meets their needs,” said Adrianne Todman, CEO
of the National Rental Home Council and former Acting Secretary of the U.S. Department of Housing and
Urban Development during the Biden Administration.

The findings come as Arizona policymakers continue to weigh housing affordability, following federal
action this past summer. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act authorized several new programs,
streamlined existing programs, like the HOME grant program, and placed limits on large institutional
investors from purchasing existing single-family homes.

“As state policymakers look ahead to 2027,” Todman said. “the opportunity is to help families find a home
that works for them, close to the jobs and communities they’ve built their lives around.”

About the survey
The survey of 600 Phoenix-area residents was conducted by Pollfish in September 2026.

items.title: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search
items.description: Renter survey: Why fee transparency matters in AI-powered property search Published Nov. 16, 2026 By Hallie Busta Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Permission granted by Zillow Sponsored content By Zillow Rentals SPONSORED CONTENT BY Fee transparency is quickly shifting from “nice to have” to a core differentiator for multifamily operators looking to stand out in a crowded market. New data from Zillow, based on a survey of more than 53,700 renters nationwide, found that nearly all (96%) want all fees disclosed, and more than three-quarters (78%) prefer they be bundled into their rent for a single, clear, all-in cost. Prospects wanting to know exactly how much it will cost to live at a property isn’t new, but the arrival of artificial intelligence (AI) in their searches is raising the stakes for operators to answer that question. Zillow found that 28% of recent renters who used AI anywhere in their search used it to negotiate — with this number rising to 37% among those renting in buildings with 50 or more units. AI search lets renters ask specific, plain language questions about a property, and its answers prioritize complete, accurate listings that include all the information renters want to know. “Growing cost concerns and rising AI use should be a catalyst for treating fee transparency as part of the decision experience, not just a disclosure requirement,” says Brian Miller, Principal for Industry & Partnership at Zillow Rentals. Renters’ priorities are shifting The data makes it clear: Today’s renter wants affordability and value. That means amenities and new finishes aren’t as attractive as they once were. Operators that can show how their property delivers on affordability and value (with or without the wellness rooms and bowling alleys ) are more likely to convert prospects into renters and keep them. Rising renter costs are fueling this shift: Security deposits are up roughly $200 year over year, and the share of renters paying at least 1 recurring fee other than for pets rose 11 points during that time, according to the survey data. Meanwhile, the data indicate renters are factoring in their commute and walkability more than before — unsurprising, as fuel prices remain high and volatile across the country. AI is elevating renters’ fee transparency demands AI is changing property search by letting prospects ask highly specific questions to help them decide whether your property meets their needs before they even step foot on-site. Operators should be mindful of this trend: a significant majority (78%) of recent renters used AI at least once during the searching, shopping, or renting process . Top uses for AI during property search, according to Zillow’s survey of recent renters: Home recommendations: 56% Personalized answers about their lease: 45% (for renters at 50+ unit properties, that jumps to 53%) Market insights: 44% Help deciding whether to rent or buy: 37% Negotiating on their behalf: 28% (37% for renters at 50+ unit properties) Zillow AI mode data shows today’s prospective renters are asking about cost early in the process. “Pricing and fees” is the third-most-common search topic in AI mode, following location and amenities. Renters want to know more than the advertised “monthly rent.” They expect to see information about fees, utilities, required deposits, parking, internet access, and other recurring expenses. Clear, consistent cost information across listings is essential for operators that want to stay competitive in the new world of AI-enabled property search. Property comparisons account for 40% of recent renter prompts in Zillow’s AI mode. That’s evidence renters are turning to AI to answer a question listings too often leave unresolved: Which home is right for me, and what will it actually cost to live there? What this means for operators AI is a new path to discovery and consideration. The more detailed the listing, especially in how it anticipates prospects’ affordability concerns, the more likely it is to be found by AI and influence renters’ decisions. To ensure property listings include the affordability information that renters want and that AI tools will look for, operators should: Show the full required monthly cost upfront. Clearly separate mandatory charges from optional add-ons and one-time fees. Keep cost information consistent wherever a property is listed. “Renters cite evaluating and comparing properties as their biggest pain point nearly twice as often as they do finding listings,” Miller says. “Hidden fees, inconsistent pricing, and missing amenity details make it harder to compare, undermining trust and making it harder for renters to confidently choose their property.” Get the full picture of today’s renter AI lets prospects compare already available information about a property. But it can’t fill the information gaps operators leave. By publishing clear, detailed, and consistent information about all costs associated with a property on every platform it’s advertised, operators can ensure their properties show up where renters are looking — and with the right information to answer questions and move renters forward in their consideration. Download the full report to learn more about how today’s renters are approaching search and what they’re looking for in properties. items.description: Oregon Neighborhood Center Acquired for $25.5M by Texas Investor A Dallas, Texas-based real estate entity acquired Gresham Square, an 85,881-square-foot neighborhood shopping center in Gresham, Oregon, within the Portland metropolitan area. The property traded for $25.5 million, or $297 per square foot. Originally developed in 1973, the center sits on 8.72 acres at 56-360 Northwest Burnside Road. It is anchored by Wunderland, a longtime Oregon family entertainment operator, and features a diverse tenant roster that includes Raising Cane's, Red Lobster, Dutch Bros. Coffee, Kaiser Permanente Dental Office, Providence Rehabilitation Services, Vancouver Clinic with Humana, Edward Jones and Plato's Closet. Gresham Square was sold by Cumberland Holdings LLC, which acquired the property in 2014. The company made significant improvements to the center, including upgrading the façade and landscaping, expanding the Wunderland tenant from 8,000 to 38,000 square feet, and demolishing a 40,000-square-foot furniture store to create a 1.5-acre subdivided parcel leased to Raising Cane's. Hanley Investment Group 's Kevin Fryman, in association with ParaSell, Inc., represented Cumberland Holdings in the transaction. The buyer represented themselves. items.description: HAR named among defendants in new Compass litigation by Emily Marek November 16, 2026 HAR is one of 15 MLSs named in a new slate of Compass lawsuits. Compass filed new antitrust lawsuits against 15 different MLSs, with the Houston Association of REALTORS ’® Houston Realtors Information Service, Inc., named among the defendants. All MLSs named in Compass’ new slate of suits have rules that require real estate agents to share listings with the MLS when they begin publicly marketing those properties, a practice that directly contradicts Compass’ highly contested three-phase marketing strategy . “Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass representative said in a press release. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.” In its complaint against HAR, Compass called the association a “competition-killing real estate industry organization” and asserted that HRIS and its “co-conspirators” have banded together to “deprive homeowners of choice.” In addition to HAR, the listing services named in Compass lawsuits include: Arizona Regional MLS bridgeMLS Bay East MLS Canopy MLS Contra Costa MLS Doorify MLS Hive MLS MLSListings The MLS-CLAW NorthstarMLS OneKey MLS REcolorado San Diego MLS Stellar MLS Compass maintains that the lawsuits will ultimately decide whether homeowners or MLSs get to decide how properties are marketed. “It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” the Compass representative added. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?” HAR declined to comment. items.description: The coming week holds a packed slate of insights from Realtor.com Economics, as well as vital indicators about the state of the housing market. On Monday, senior economist Jiayi Xu published a report on free and clear mortgages , which breaks down trends in where the most homeowners own their home outright . On Tuesday, senior economist Joel Berner has our third-quarter New-Construction Insights report looking at how new-home prices and homebuilder incentives have trended in the past quarter. Then on Wednesday, Jiayi is back with a look at October rent trends in our monthly rental report, which will also dive deep into how apartment supply shifts are likely to affect the market. Finally, on Thursday, senior economist Anthony Smith will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest trends. Turning to the macro indicators that will be released, both pending home sales and new construction will be released on Wednesday and on Thursday, we’ll see mortgage rates. October pending home sales, released by the National Association of Realtors®, are likely to be low. In September, the pending data hit a series record low , tumbling more than 7% in the month and 11% from a year ago. Realtor.com data showed double-digit declines in both pending sales and new contract signings in October. I think we’re likely to see another tough few months for housing activity as we wrap up 2026. In September’s construction report from the U.S. Census Bureau, permits, starts, and completions all fell from both the prior month and prior year. items.description: Roughly 3 in 5 American homeowners pay a mortgage every month, yet the share of those who own their property outright is steadily growing—with at least half of all homeowners in three states now completely mortgage-free . According to a new Realtor.com® data analysis of the recently released 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates , 59% of homeowners carried a mortgage last year, while 41% owned their homes free and clear. That marks a major shift from 2010, when fewer than a third of homes (32.8%) were owned outright while 67% carried home loan debt. Mortgaged homeownership has shrunk across all four regions, though reliance on financing still varies significantly by geography. The West had the highest mortgage debt rate at 63.8%, while the South recorded the lowest at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest tied at 58.7%. At the state level, West Virginia led the nation with 56.6% of its homeowners living mortgage-free, followed by Mississippi (52.7%) and New Mexico (50%). On the other side of the spectrum, Washington, DC, in 2025 logged the lowest share of outright homeownership, at just 26.5%, trailed by Maryland (30.6%) and Colorado (31.6%). Loading... Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu explains that the balance between mortgaged and free-and-clear homes meaningfully shapes housing market dynamics, especially at a time when mortgage rates are high. "Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs," says Xu. "Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs." Ultimately, those market forces sway inventory levels, home prices, and whether first-time buyers can access homeownership. With mortgage rates stuck above 7% and the Federal Reserve all but certain to raise interest rates in December—and possibly again in January 2027—to combat inflation, the lock-in effect is poised to chill the market again . Homeowners sitting on low mortgage rates are reluctant to give them up, keeping much-needed inventory off the market. That supply squeeze, in turn, puts upward pressure on prices and makes it harder for renters to access homeownership. Free-and-clear owners, however, are not bound by borrowing costs and can list whenever they choose. "A mortgage-free owner isn’t watching interest rates to decide when to move," Christie Goldman , a real estate agent with Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in Charleston, WV , tells Realtor.com. "They can buy their next home with cash, which makes their offer stronger, and they can close on their own timeline without a lender, an appraisal contingency, or rate risk." Loading... The Mountain State leads the way Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, West Virginia stands out with the lowest share of mortgaged homes, at 43.4%, and conversely the highest share of outright ownership, at 56.6%. Two main forces drive this dynamic: relatively low median home prices and an older population that tends to hold on to properties longer than residents in many other states. "In West Virginia, a paid-off home isn’t a someday goal. It's how people here live," says Goldman. "When people put down roots here, they stay." It is common for a local family to purchase a home, raise their children there, and pay it off, often with the next generation buying property in the same community. According to Goldman, affordability is what makes that cycle possible. In October 2026, the median asking price in West Virginia was $259,999, well below the national median of $415,000. "At those prices, owning your home free and clear is a realistic goal here, not a distant dream," says the agent, pointing to the 2025 United Van Lines’ national study that ranked West Virginia as the second-leading inbound destination for movers. "Many of those buyers sell a higher-priced home elsewhere and can pay cash here," says Goldman. "Once they discover the mountains, the community, and the pace of life, they don’t want to leave." Loading... West Virgina has the nation's highest share of homeowners who own property outright, at nearly 57%. Posnov/Getty Images Xu also attributes West Virginia's high share of mortgage-free owners to the state's slow population growth, particularly among young adults, which has kept new borrowers from entering the market in large numbers. Between 2015 and 2025, the population aged 18–34 fell 5% in West Virginia, while the same age group in the U.S. grew 3.8%. Owning one's home outright offers many perks, sharply reducing monthly expenses and creating a buffer against economic headwinds. "Mortgage-free homeowners have more financial flexibility, especially with today's higher interest rates and rising living costs," Thomas O’Shaughnessy , vice president and real estate broker at Clever Real Estate , tells Realtor.com. "They don't have monthly mortgage payments, which makes it easier to manage expenses, save money, and handle unexpected repairs or emergencies." In theory, a high percentage of debt-free homeowners can also help unlock inventory for the next wave of buyers. items.title: CCM leader Brady Mullen's playbook to win reverse mortgage referrals without a hard sales pitch
items.description: Brady Mullen, divisional business development manager for CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM), spent 20 years as a financial adviser before selling his practice in 2021. In his experience, advisers are rarely trained on how to properly handle real estate, the biggest asset owned by most of their clients. In seeking to close that gap, Mullen changed his career trajectory by moving into reverse mortgages, first at American Liberty Mortgage before his arrival at CCM in late 2024. He believes that reverse mortgages are the most misunderstood and underappreciated financial tools on the market. In his work to grow reverse mortgage originations at one of the nation's largest independent mortgage banks, Mullen has focused on helping loan officers build a steady stream of referral partners, including financial planners, real estate agents and attorneys. That task often meets resistance as referral sources can have the same stigmas about the products as consumers. At last week's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Conference & Expo and San Antonio, Mullen discussed ways to create stronger referral networks. His advice in a nutshell? Take what works and let go of the rest. Plant, nourish, harvest Mullen chooses to organize his business development efforts in similar fashion to a farmer growing crops. Planting season involves prospecting and presentations. Fertilizing and nourishing involves follow-up conversations. Harvesting is what occurs when the leads arrive. Each of the three stages includes its own subprocesses, he explained, a structure that allows a loan officer or branch manager to see where leads stall and fix the bottleneck. When interacting with a potential referral source, Mullen suggests that reverse mortgage professionals remove words like "educate" and "teach" from their vocabulary. Telling another adult that "I want to educate you" sounds condescending, he said. Instead, offer a benefit that has nothing to do with money, such as continuing education credits. "If it's structured as CE, you've set the tone to have a discussion that, by design, was created by you to go through the topics in the order that you want and to deliver them with the visuals," Mullen said. Mullen told the NRMLA audience that advice on money-making activities should not be part of referral partner conversations. Other professionals know how to make money, he said, and people who have misconceptions about the product are likely to be turned off by the phrase, "Here's how I can help you make money." Instead, frame the discussion around providing answers. A financial adviser's clients, for example, may want to know how they can help their parents or grandparents. "You're not trying to sell reverse mortgages. You're not trying to get a referral. What are you trying to get? A presentation. … That's all you want. Don't ask for more because you'll spoil the opportunity," he explained. Validate, inform, call to action Once the seeds have been planted and a referral partner has agreed to learn more, reverse mortgages professionals should create an arc with their presentations. The first step is validation, as referrals partners won't recommend something they won't use themselves. With Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), emphasize the built-in protections of mortgage insurance premiums . Someone clinging to the idea that reverse mortgages are scams needs to know about their robust regulations through the Federal Housing Administration and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau . He also calls for simplified language. Describe the HECM product as an expanding line of credit and avoid creating confusion by explaining principal limit factors. Outline the key features that define every reverse mortgage — optional monthly payments , no balloon payments and nonrecourse provisions. From there, give a clear explanation of the financial benefits for borrowers. He used the example of a $300,000 loan at a 7% rate. A forward mortgage that amortizes over 15 years costs roughly $2,700 a month, while a 30-year loan costs about $2,000 a month. Interest-only options may only trim a few hundred dollars per month. But reverse mortgages do not require a payment and can be more efficient in terms of opportunity costs. For instance, a 75-year-old couple can take $50,000 out of a retirement account or they can borrow it, but their net worth is still the same. Borrowing offers the potential added benefits of tax savings and asset control. "Your balance sheet doesn't care whether it's paying an opportunity cost or interest. It treats them indifferently. It's going to reflect both of those equally," Mullen said. "If we're not looking at the other side of the balance sheet, we're missing half the picture, and that's a lot of picture for an expert to miss." For the right type of referral relationship, Mullen believes that longer educational videos, rather than shorter sound bites, are more helpful. He said his most popular YouTube video on reverse mortgages is 43 minutes long. When assigned as homework before a meeting, this type of content allows the referral partner to fully absorb the concepts and share them with clients, who can potentially screen themselves out without further time and energy spent by the LO. To properly nurture these relationships, Mullen says to contact them every two to three weeks. Don't worry if people unsubscribe from marketing campaigns , since this will allow you to focus on engaged prospects. "Would you rather have a distribution list of 1,000 and very little engagement, or a distribution list of 80 and have a lot of engagement? The second is by far more effective," Mullen said. items.title: Villa hires former Century Communities CFO Messenger as CEO
items.description: Villa , a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company announced on Monday. Founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods. The company manages feasibility, design, permitting, site preparation and installation, and partners with a network of factories for production, according to the announcement. Messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities . During his tenure, Century expanded from about 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states, grew to $4.5 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,000 annual closings, completed seven acquisitions and raised more than $3 billion in debt and equity capital, the company said. He also led Century’s initial public offering and helped launch its mortgage, title and insurance subsidiaries, giving him direct experience with the vertically integrated models many large homebuilders use to manage costs and capture more of the housing value chain. Earlier in his career, Messenger spent roughly a decade at UDR , a publicly traded multifamily real estate investment trust, where he advanced through senior finance roles to become CFO. Messenger’s appointment comes as Villa looks to expand beyond individual ADUs and small projects into larger communities in partnership with land developers and homebuilders. The company is already working on new neighborhoods including the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado, and homes in Altadena, California, for families rebuilding after the Eaton Fire, according to the release. Investors say his background in scaling a public homebuilder and in capital markets was a key factor in the decision. “Villa has demonstrated its capabilities across ADUs, multifamily properties and new neighborhoods, and Dave is the right leader to build on Villa’s success and advance its growth strategy,” said Aaron Marsh, partner and CFO at Unless, an investor in Villa and member of Villa’s board of directors. “He brings deep housing experience, a track record of scaling businesses nationally and a clear understanding of what land and development partners need to move projects forward.” Messenger said he sees an opportunity to apply processes from large-scale homebuilding to Villa’s offsite platform. “This team has done what much of our industry has only talked about: delivering quality homes through offsite construction across individual properties, multifamily communities and new neighborhoods,” Messenger said in the announcement. “I see great potential to build on that foundation by bringing a large-scale homebuilder’s operating discipline to Villa, with an emphasis on predictable execution and profitable growth.” Villa’s model aims to give homeowners, multifamily operators and developers a single partner from concept through completion. The company handles site feasibility, site and home design, permitting and on-site work and uses factory partners to build homes offsite, aiming for more predictable timelines and costs than traditional stick-built construction, according to the release. “Dave has an exceptional track record spanning homebuilding, multifamily real estate, capital markets and land development,” said Heather Miksch, chief operating officer at Villa. “As we build on Villa’s momentum and pursue development opportunities, his experience will be invaluable in helping us grow our business while continuing to serve both homeowners and development partners.” Related More: homebuilder Real Estate

items.title: Macerich Acquires Oakridge Mall In San Jose For $250M
items.description: Google Maps Macerich purchased the Oakridge mall in San Jose. Macerich acquired the 1.1M SF Oakridge mall in San Jose’s Blossom Valley neighborhood for approximately $250M. The acquisition of the mall at 925 Blossom Hill Road will be funded entirely through equity from the sale of 11 million shares of common stock in June for $23.12 per share, Macerich said in a release . The acquisition significantly expands Macerich’s footprint in the Bay Area. The REIT also owns the 996K SF Broadway Plaza mall in Walnut Creek and the 501K SF The Village at Corte Madera in Marin County. Companies signed about 26K SF of new leases at Oakridge in 2026, and another 70K SF is in negotiations, according to Macerich. If these leases go forward as expected, the mall will be roughly 90% occupied. “Oakridge Mall is a highly productive retail center doing approximately $866 inline sales per square foot located within one of the wealthiest markets in the country,” Macerich President and CEO Jackson Hsieh said in the release. The single-level enclosed mall anchored by Macy’s, 99 Ranch Marketplace, Target and Cinemark Theatres generated roughly $400M in retail sales for the 12 months ended Sept. 30, Macerich noted. Nearly 11 million people visit the mall annually, the company added. Former owner Unibail-Rodamco-Westfield originally listed Oakridge for sale in early 2024 in an effort to streamline its portfolio, the Silicon Valley Business Journal reported . Macerich said the acquisition is expected to add 2 cents per share to its 2028 target funds from operations and deliver 30 cents per share once the mall is fully stabilized. “Our plan is to add even more compelling experiences, entertainment, dining and wellness concepts that encourage engagement, further increase dwell time/foot traffic and give customers even more reasons to visit the center,” Hsieh said. Macerich’s acquisition comes as San Jose’s retail market continues to tighten. Overall vacancy in the third quarter of 2026 was 3.2%, down 80 basis points from the same quarter a year earlier, Kidder Mathews reported . Despite negative net absorption of nearly 70K SF in Q3, year-to-date net absorption stands at a net positive 586K SF. A thin construction pipeline of new retail buildings in Silicon Valley is expected to further compress vacancy rates, Kidder Mathews researchers noted. items.description: A fledgling company led by a right-wing political operative is raising money for a half-million-square-foot mixed-use project in Tysons featuring a for-profit conservative institute. Its vision includes a center “for high culture in innovation and science,” a 165-room hotel, up to 200 apartments, office, retail and restaurant space, a park, a public atrium and a chapel theater. items.title: Alex Vidal to oversee REMAX Canada as company clarifies remit
items.description: Not only is Alex Vidal the new president of REMAX , but the company has clarified that his appointment to this position also encompasses REMAX Canada, making him the leader of REMAX’s Canadian operation. Vidal was named president of REMAX in September, after The Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of REMAX, forming the Real REMAX Group . In an emailed statement, a REMAX spokesperson told HousingWire that the president of REMAX has always overseen the company’s Canadian operation. As Vidal moves into the Canadian leadership position, Don Kottick, who has served as the president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, has announced plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15. This information was conveyed to REMAX brokers and franchisees via an internal memo reviewed and confirmed by HousingWire. “This move helps ensure every REMAX region around the world receives as much of the same focus, momentum and opportunities as possible,” the internal memo stated. “The next few months will be pivotal as we roll out new technology and invest in further strengthening the REMAX brand in Canada and around the world.” Prior to joining REMAX, Kottick was the president and CEO of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada . Before joining REMAX, Vidal served as the president of ERA Real Estate , helping lead the brand through Compass International Holdings ’s acquisition of its parent company Anywhere Real Estate . Compass and ERA are currently suing Vidal , claiming that he violated non-compete agreements through his move to REMAX. In the legal complaint filed in mid-October, Compass claims that the non-compete agreement prevents Vidal from serving as president or providing service to any competing business for a period of one year from his departure from ERA. items.title: Amid ‘economic headwinds,’ Boston looks to ease its inclusionary zoning policy
items.description: Amid ‘economic headwinds,’ Boston looks to ease its inclusionary zoning policy The city is proposing reduced developer fees and higher thresholds for affordable housing mandates. Published Nov. 16, 2026 Ryan Kushner Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Boston Mayor Michelle Wu on Nov. 10, 2026, proposed a number of changes to the city's inclusionary zoning policy to encourage more development. Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 2 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Dive Brief: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu last week proposed easing the city’s inclusionary zoning requirements “in the continued face of economic headwinds,” according to a news release. Proposed changes include reducing developer payment-in-lieu fees, extending affordable housing payment schedules and temporarily raising the threshold from seven units to 10 for the size of multifamily housing that must participate. “By providing greater flexibility and reducing upfront costs, we can help make more housing and commercial development financially feasible while preserving the affordability requirements that are so important to Boston’s future,” Boston Chief of Planning Kairos Shen said in a statement. Dive Insight: In a subdued housing market , more cities are adjusting affordable housing mandates for developers. San Francisco this summer slashed its affordable housing requirements for multifamily developers from 15% of units to 5%, according to Mission Local. New Orleans reduced its per-unit affordable housing fee by more than 96% — from $304,810 to $10,000, New Orleans City Business reported last month. Boston’s inclusionary zoning policies, which require 17% of qualifying multifamily units to be income-restricted, have produced nearly 3,000 affordable housing units over the past five years, according to Wu. Wu’s proposal cuts condominium payment-in-lieu fees — fees paid to the city when a developer does not include required affordable units — from 75% to 50% of the difference between market-rate and income-restricted unit values. Developers also could spread out those payments across seven installments instead of two. “This balanced approach is part of our administration’s broader strategy to build more homes, remove barriers to development, and ensure Boston remains a city where residents can afford to stay and thrive,” Wu said. The Boston Planning Department advanced the proposal Nov. 12. Now it will go before the Boston Zoning Commission and the City Council for approval. “We recognize that the cost of building housing has increased, and we want to be responsive to these realities,” Boston Chief of Housing Sheila Dillon said in a news release. “These program changes are designed to encourage the development of new housing while maintaining our commitment to affordability.” Recommended Reading These 3 housing programs are showing results. items.title: Realpage’s New York lawsuit tests the limits of algorithmic rent-pricing bans
items.description: Realpage’s New York lawsuit tests the limits of algorithmic rent-pricing bans RealPage Inc. v. James “could provide meaningful guidance on how far state and local governments can go in regulating or restricting these technologies,” a lawyer told Multifamily Dive. Published Nov. 16, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Scott Heins via Getty Images Listen to the article 6 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . A lawsuit regarding New York state’s algorithmic rent-setting ban is testing how far the government can go in restricting such tools without also overly impeding commercial speech, and may provide more clarity about what is within legal bounds, legal experts say. Although it’s difficult to estimate how influential the ultimate decision in RealPage Inc. v. James will be, the preliminary ruling indicates “the case could provide meaningful guidance on how far state and local governments can go in regulating or restricting these technologies without running afoul of the First Amendment,” Corinne Migliazza, associate at real estate law firm Otten Johnson, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. In 2024, the Department of Justice and several states sued Realpage and several major landlords that used its pricing product, alleging in United States et al. v. RealPage Inc. et al. that the use of algorithmic software to coordinate rents violated antitrust law. As settlements from that case started rolling out, New York became the first state, in 2025, to impose an outright ban on residential rent-pricing algorithms with its antitrust law amendment S.7882 . Before New York’s ban was set to take effect last year, Realpage went on the offensive. It sued the state in November 2025 on free speech grounds rather than making antitrust arguments. Then it asked the court to halt the ban while its case was being heard. The federal judge agreed to grant a preliminary injunction at the end of September and also denied the state’s January request to dismiss the lawsuit. Judge Valerie Caproni said that some language of the ban likely restricts protected speech more broadly than necessary because it is “undiscerning in targeting software without regard to its use of public versus non-public data.” Although the judge indicated the decision would be a close call, her ruling hints that the court is skeptical of New York’s restrictions, “at least enough to allow more evidence and fact to be developed and presented,” according to Migliazza. “There are also suggestions that the Court may be more receptive to narrowly tailored restrictions, like the initial RealPage settlements, which restricted the algorithms to publicly available information, rather than prohibiting their use outright,” Migliazza said. It remains to be seen whether the court will address particular uses of algorithmic rent-pricing tools in depth. It may decide to only rule on the constitutionality of New York’s restrictions and put the ball in the legislature’s court to find a better solution, according to Migliazza. “Certainly, a First Amendment victory by RealPage would force the legislature back to the drawing board to contour the law towards constitutionality – meaning they would have to make the restrictions less severe,” Migliazza said. New York case impact Algorithmic rent-pricing restrictions are proliferating: New Jersey’s FAIR Act is set to take effect on July 1, 2027, although it is structured differently from New York’s law. Jersey City, New Jersey; Providence, Rhode Island; Philadelphia; Minneapolis; San Francisco; Seattle; Rockville, Maryland, have also passed similar measures. That growing patchwork of algorithmic pricing laws is making compliance more complicated for the rental housing industry, Peter Carstensen, antitrust expert and professor of law emeritus at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, told Multifamily Dive. “What's a developer to do, especially if those regulations are in some way contrary to each other?” Carstensen said. It’s important for rental housing firms to follow these information exchange lawsuits and antitrust litigation more broadly, and to ask, “What are the red lights or the yellow lights that we need to watch out for? How do we make sure that people down in marketing are not creating problems for us?” according to Carstensen. Indeed, landlords are not necessarily in the clear to use algorithmic pricing tools, legal experts at law firm Lowenstein Sandler wrote. They urged caution in New York, and said to prepare for changes in New Jersey and varied algorithmic pricing laws more generally. “Tools that pool competitors’ nonpublic data, discourage price reductions, standardize lease terms, or otherwise limit independent decision-making should be closely reviewed,” according to Lowenstein Sandler. Consultation on the front end to ensure compliance with the relevant jurisdiction’s regulations could save a lot of time, energy and money later on, according to Migliazza, particularly as such regulations continue to evolve. “There is no doubt that as the technological landscape surrounding artificial intelligence changes, the legal one will too,” she said. A few weeks following the court’s decision to halt the state’s ban, New York Attorney General Letitia James asked the judge to reconsider and vacate the injunction, per an Oct. 13 filing in the U.S. District Court, Southern District of New York. items.title: Craig Hall Is Betting on the Future of Office. His Next Chapter at HALL Park Is Taking Shape.
items.description: Live Poll At a time when many commercial real estate developers are hesitant to break ground on new office buildings, Craig Hall is doing just that. The entrepreneur and founder of HALL Group is moving forward with the next phase of HALL Park, his 162-acre development in Frisco, with a new Class A office tower, an expansion of the popular Kaleidoscope Park, and additional residential development. The investment comes as HALL Park is experiencing renewed leasing momentum, including a major commitment from JPMorganChase and the recent relocation of Public Storage's corporate headquarters from California to HALL Park. For Hall, who began developing HALL Park more than three decades ago, the activity represents another milestone in a much larger vision: transforming what began as a suburban office campus into a thriving mixed-use district where people can work, live, dine, and spend time outside the office. And while the broader office market continues to face questions about demand, construction costs, and the future of the workplace, HALL Group is positioning itself for what it believes will be the next cycle of growth. A Different Kind of Office Market The commercial office market has experienced a fundamental shift in recent years. Remote and hybrid work have changed how companies use their space, while higher construction costs and interest rates have made new development increasingly difficult to justify. But the slowdown in construction may be creating an opportunity for developers willing to take a longer-term view. Across North Texas, relatively few new speculative office buildings are moving forward. At the same time, companies seeking modern, high-quality workplaces are increasingly looking for environments that offer more than traditional office space. HALL Group is betting that this combination of limited future supply and continued demand for premium workplaces will create favorable conditions for its next generation of development. The company's confidence is supported by leasing activity at HALL Park, where several major corporations have recently committed to space. In August, JPMorganChase announced plans to lease approximately 41,000 square feet at The Tower HALL Park, bringing 120 bankers from its commercial banking, private banking, and wealth management divisions to Frisco. The company plans to occupy the space in early 2028, establishing a prominent presence in the 16-story office tower. The recent activity builds on an established corporate tenant base that includes companies such as Public Storage, Deloitte, and Altair Global, reinforcing HALL Park's appeal to both national corporations and growing businesses seeking a presence in North Texas. The commitments are particularly significant given the challenges facing the broader office sector. They suggest that while companies may be reconsidering how much office space they need, demand remains for well-located, highly amenitized buildings that can help attract employees and serve clients. For HALL Group, the leasing momentum also provides a foundation for its next major investment. Building When Others Aren't Construction is underway on The Terraces HALL Park, a 10-story office tower that will bring more than 200,000 square feet of new Class A space to the development. Designed and constructed by The Beck Group, the building represents HALL Group's latest approach to the evolving workplace, emphasizing flexibility, hospitality, and outdoor access. Private terraces will extend from every floor, while a dedicated amenity level will feature meeting spaces, a lounge and bar, and an expansive outdoor terrace overlooking Kaleidoscope Park. Perhaps more notable is how the building's office space will be delivered. Approximately 60% of The Terraces will consist of fully finished, move-in-ready suites, catering to small and midsized companies seeking high-quality space without the time and expense of designing and constructing their own offices. The remaining space will offer customizable options for larger tenants. The strategy reflects a shift in corporate real estate preferences. Rather than committing to large, unfinished spaces and lengthy buildouts, many businesses are prioritizing flexibility, convenience, and workplaces that are ready for immediate use. items.title: A NorthPark Coffee Crawl
items.description: Live Poll I’m a street walker. You heard right. If there’s a street in an Italian city, I’ll walk it. Verona, for me, is the quintessential Italian walking town. There are two piazzas, Piazza Bra and Piazza delle Erbe, linked by a well-worn pathway—don’t try walking on it in a rainstorm; you will slip and fall—filled with the well-known fashion boutiques of Italy and France. And of course the street is dotted with countless coffee and gelato shops, which are frequented by the locals who stroll about unhurriedly. In the car-forward culture of Dallas, it’s a rare sight. But there is one place I’ve found where I can recreate a little speck of Italy. And for coffee lovers, this is a mecca. In 1965, Raymond Nasher opened an indoor shopping plaza, NorthPark Center, that approaches the Italian retail and coffee experience in spirit. You may not think of NorthPark as a coffee destination, but consider this: the possibilities run from seasonal favorites at Starbucks or Ebar by Nordstrom to places like La La Land Kind Cafe and Caffè Lavazza at Eataly , where the caffeinated concoctions range from deeply traditional ones coming out of Torino to the sun-drenched fantasies of the Left Coast. Guides The Definitive Dallas Coffee Guide Dallas is a city of coffee fanatics, aficionados, and nerds. Find your favorite. By Eve Hill-Agnus | January 12, 2026 | 6:22 pm Many of us got our introduction to coffee culture via Starbucks , and for novices and disciples alike, it’s still the default. But I am painfully introverted, so when I see the lines and all the people, I have the perfect pivot. Fewer than 150 steps away from the East Wing location is a second Starbucks. Find it, sans the line, on the second level just inside Macy’s , where you can score an espresso or a seasonal coffee drink, be it pecan, pumpkin, or peppermint. An introvert’s dream. My other walking town, Torino, is a city tourists often skip on their way through Italy. Pity, for it is to the Piedmont wine region what San Francisco is to Napa and Sonoma. It is also a coffee and chocolate pilgrimage destination, and where I had my first Bicerin—layer upon layer of espresso, hot chocolate and cold cream. Eataly was born in Torino in 2007 and has since expanded all over the world, including to Dallas. Caffè Lavazza at Eataly (first level) is all about the classic specialty coffee drinks that Italians adore. Find your Bicerin there. Caffé Lavazza's marble top espresso bar with its own cappuccino station (aka where the coffee magic is made). Courtesy Eataly Dallas While you’re at the register, notice the sign offering a caffè sospeso. That means you pay for two coffees and drink one, leaving the second “suspended” for whoever comes in and needs it, no questions asked. It’s a Neapolitan practice —an act of kindness handed down by word of mouth, revived after the war, and brought to Dallas when Caffè Lavazza opened in 2021. Getting a coffee at La La Land Kind Cafe is like sitting in the gate line at Burning Man—prepare to chill a bit. There are always hopeful javaphiles and tea devotees queuing for a Banana Cloud Latte or a French Toast Latte, fueled by espresso or matcha, depending on one’s preferred octane. Italy never saw anything like it, but here we are in the age of the oat-milk cloud. I bet you didn’t know there’s a secret spot at NorthPark where lounging guests get a complimentary macchiato. I’d love to tell you, but then it wouldn’t be a secret. (Hint: I have left enough clues for attentive gumshoes to crack the case.) For coffee connoisseurs curious about how to pull a proper ristretto or build a better flat white, a couple of places will teach you the finer points of foam and crema, and sell you a machine to make your own. Between Neiman Marcus and Nordstrom on level one, you’ll find Nespresso and Williams Sonoma . Both carry machines for the home barista, and both offer classes in making the perfect cappuccino. Italians have mastered the aperitivo hour. Why else are outdoor cafés always filled with folks sipping spritzes? For caffeine-crazed souls who want a little more punch in the throttle, there are espresso martinis. They swarm NorthPark, where most every spirit-pouring restaurant has its own version, and the local buzz says Joey Dallas makes one of the best in the city. Who knew espresso martinis were such a pervasive species? If you’re like me and have a sweet tooth, you can chase dinner with an affogato (Italian for “drowned”), espresso poured over a scoop of gelato, typically fior di latte. Eataly’s Terra on the third floor, La Pizza and La Pasta on the second, or the gelato bar by the east entrance will satisfy the urge. You can also pause for an affogato at Paciugo , the gelato stand on the second level where the casual cafés converge. It’s a necessary indulgence, from time to time. They say Europeans outlive us because they walk so much. Italians have the ritual of the passeggiata , a leisurely after-dinner stroll through the town piazza (or, in this case, NorthPark Center, my stand-in for Verona). Thirty years ago, if you’d told me Texas would one day embrace coffee culture the way I saw it in Italy, I wouldn’t have placed a bet. But what I saw in Seattle in those years (drive-through espresso kiosks!) foretold a wave that eventually reached our state. I still get a laugh out of folks sipping hot coffee in the dead of summer, though we’ve stretched our iced-tea habit to coffee, too. Now we can stay cool and caffeinated out of our minds, and we don’t have to hop on a dreaded plane to Italy for the perfect espresso. items.description: Live Poll The period for lawmakers (and lawmakers-elect) to pre-file bills in the Texas Legislature kicked off last week. Roughly 1,500 measures have been filed between last Monday and Friday, with the bulk (1,260) being filed on the first day. The last day to file a bill is March 12. That’s a somewhat slower pace than at the start of the last session, and the makeup of the Legislature is still taking shape after a wave of Democratic wins. As of today, in House District 61, just 134 votes separate Republican incumbent Keresa Richardson of McKinney and Democratic challenger Brittany Black. In House District 67, Democrat Jordan Wheatley trails Republican incumbent Jeff Leach of Plano by 204 votes. Five statewide wins will also open seats in the Legislature. State Sen. Nathan Johnson is now attorney general-elect, and state Sen. Sarah Eckhardt is comptroller-elect. State representatives Gina Hinojosa, James Talarico, and Vikki Goodwin will leave open seats in the Texas House after winning their elections for governor, U.S. Senate, and lieutenant governor. All five have the option of resigning now or waiting until they take office in their new roles—the sitting governor will call a special election to fill their terms. In the last legislative session, more than 8,700 bills were filed. To give an idea of how difficult it is to get a bill to the governor’s desk and signed into law, around 1,200 actually reached outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott’s desk, and he vetoed a few dozen. The process of passing a bill in Texas goes far beyond anything you heard on Schoolhouse Rock!, and each chamber has its own workflow. But it goes something like this in both chambers: a bill is filed, reviewed, and then sent to an applicable committee. The committee then debates it and decides whether to vote to pass it on to the Calendars committee, which will decide whether to schedule it for a floor debate. Following the debate, the bill must be passed by a majority of both chambers. Once it has passed in the chamber where it began, it moves on to the other to repeat the process. If both chambers pass the bill, then a committee consisting of state senators and state representatives will meet to reconcile the two bills. Once both sides have signed off on those changes, it heads to the governor's desk for signing. And all of this must be done by sine die—the day the regular legislative session ends, which is May 31. Here are a few of the bills that we’ll be watching this legislative session. As the Texas Legislature convenes in January, we will once again launch our bill tracker. (You can bookmark that here , and we’ll also send out an alert when it is updated.) High speed rail High speed rail has been a real will-they-or-won’t-they for Texas, with the appetite varying from session to session. Currently, it does not seem that the Trump administration is all that bullish on it, and it’s been a state legislative non-starter among lawmakers who are getting an earful from property owners along proposed rail sites. State Rep. John Bucy has filed House Bill 270 , which would direct TxDOT to enter into an agreement with a private company to build and operate a high-speed rail line connecting Dallas, Waco, Austin, and San Antonio along I-35. It would also repeal a part of the state transportation code that prevents state money being used to plan, build, or operate high speed rail run by a private company. (Another bill, Senate Bill 371 , would pave the way for passenger rail between Houston and Austin.) Advocates say it’s a good way for less wealthy students to afford more options, especially if their public schools are not meeting their needs or are performing poorly. Opponents say that the funding would be better spent improving public schools. Several lawmakers filed bills that would eliminate the program, including HB 164 , HB 646 , HB 1081 , HB 1093 , HB 1129 , and SB 294 , which was filed by state Sen. Royce West (D-Dallas).
